NOTICE TO AN ALLEGED FATHER IN AN ADOPTION PROCEEDING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Riley Lee · May 3, 2025

NOTICE TO AN ALLEGED FATHER IN AN ADOPTION PROCEEDING — FACTS DECLARATION
This information sheet describes California's statutory process, under California Family Code Division 12, Part 3, Chapter 5 (§§ 7660–7671), for identifying and giving notice to a man alleged to be the biological father of Riley Lee (born May 3, 2025) — identified in this document as Casey Alex — in connection with an adoption of Riley Lee that Jordan Lee, the child's birth parent, has relinquished for, consented to, or proposes to relinquish for or consent to, or in connection with which Riley Lee otherwise becomes the subject of an adoption proceeding contemplated for filing in the California superior court for Sacramento County.

California does not maintain a centralized "putative father registry" of the kind found in a number of other states — a state database in which a man who believes he may have fathered a child affirmatively registers his own identifying information in advance, before any specific adoption is filed, to preserve a right to later notice. The California mechanism described in this document's companion clauses instead works in the other direction: it places an affirmative duty on the court and a state or county adoption agency to search for and identify an alleged father in connection with a specific, already-pending adoption matter, and then to give that identified alleged father actual notice of that specific proceeding, with a statutory window in which to respond.

This information sheet is not itself a court filing. Completing it does not itself identify, locate, notify, or terminate the parental rights of any alleged father, and does not determine that any specific adoption should or will be granted. Only the statutory inquiry, notice, and (where applicable) court petition process described in this document's companion clauses, followed by a court order, can actually do that.

CALIFORNIA HAS NO CENTRALIZED "PUTATIVE FATHER REGISTRY" — THE STATUTE INSTEAD IMPOSES A SEARCH-AND-NOTICE DUTY
Unlike a number of other states, California's Family Code does not establish a centralized, state-maintained registry in which a man who believes he may have fathered a child affirmatively enrolls his own identifying information, in advance of any specific adoption, to preserve a right to later notice. The California statutory chapter addressing this subject carries its own official heading, "CHAPTER 5. Termination of Parental Rights in Adoption Proceedings [7660 - 7671]" — a search-and-notice framework, not a registry. Rather than requiring an alleged father to register himself, Family Code § 7663(a) places the burden on the court: "In an effort to identify all alleged fathers and presumed parents, the court shall cause inquiry to be made of the mother and any other appropriate person by one of the following:" — and among the bodies the court may direct to carry out that inquiry, § 7663(a)(1) names "The State Department of Social Services."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "CHAPTER 5. Termination of Parental Rights in Adoption Proceedings [7660 - 7671]"
  — Cal. Fam. Code Division 12, Part 3, Chapter 5 heading, as it appears on the page for § 7660 (California Legislative Information text), the chapter's own official title (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7660.)
  "In an effort to identify all alleged fathers and presumed parents, the court shall cause inquiry to be made of the mother and any other appropriate person by one of the following:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7663(a) (California Legislative Information text), the court's duty to cause an identification inquiry (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7663.)
  "The State Department of Social Services."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7663(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), the State Department of Social Services as one body that may conduct the inquiry (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7663.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's own text structures this subject — not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific adoption, nor a claim that every state, or even most states, structures this the same way; a number of other states do maintain a proactive, self-registration putative-father registry, and this document takes no position on how any of those states' registries operate. This clause corrects a premise the underlying research request began with: California is not among the states that maintain such a registry, and no Department of Justice- or California Health and Human Services Agency-administered father-registration database was located in the current Family Code; the state office named in the statute's own text for conducting or assigning the identification inquiry is the State Department of Social Services (Family Code § 7663(a)(1)), not the Department of Justice or the Health and Human Services Agency. This clause cites the Chapter 5 heading itself (part of the same fetched page as § 7660) and two provisions of § 7663(a) (its introductory clause and paragraph (1)); the chapter heading and § 7663 are treated as two independent sources, though the two quoted parts of § 7663(a) are not independent of each other. This document does not describe every state or county agency listed in § 7663(a)(2)-(4) as alternative bodies that may conduct the inquiry in place of the department; that is addressed only in part in this document's companion clause on the inquiry itself. This document is informational only: it does not itself identify, register, or track any specific alleged father, and does not determine that the framework described in this document applies in the same way to every adoption.

WHAT THE COURT-DIRECTED INQUIRY MUST COVER IN ATTEMPTING TO IDENTIFY AN ALLEGED FATHER
The identification inquiry described in this document's companion clause is not open-ended; Family Code § 7663(b) lists specific topics it must cover: "The inquiry shall include all of the following:" and, among the five listed topics, paragraph (5) directs inquiry into "The names and whereabouts, if known, of every person presumed or alleged to be the parent of the child, and the efforts made to give notice of the proposed adoption to each person identified." Once that inquiry is complete, § 7663(c) requires that "The agency that completes the inquiry shall file a written report of the findings with the court."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The inquiry shall include all of the following:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7663(b) (California Legislative Information text), introductory clause listing what the inquiry must cover (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7663.)
  "The names and whereabouts, if known, of every person presumed or alleged to be the parent of the child, and the efforts made to give notice of the proposed adoption to each person identified."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7663(b)(5) (California Legislative Information text), inquiry into names, whereabouts, and notice efforts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7663.)
  "The agency that completes the inquiry shall file a written report of the findings with the court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7663(c) (California Legislative Information text), written report of findings filed with the court (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7663.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific topics California's own inquiry-and-report duty covers — not a claim about which state's law governs, or what inquiry, if any, another state's process requires regarding a specific child. This clause cites three parts of the same statutory section — § 7663(b)'s introductory clause, § 7663(b)(5), and § 7663(c) — and treats them as one source, not three independent ones. This clause does not restate inquiry topics (b)(1) through (4) — whether the mother was married or cohabiting with a man at the relevant times, whether she received support payments or promises of support, and whether any person has formally or informally acknowledged possible parentage — which this document's companion clause on the no-registry framework references only in passing. This document is informational only: it does not itself conduct any inquiry, does not identify or locate any specific alleged father, and does not determine what an inquiry into the facts of the child named in this document's companion clauses would find.

NOTICE TO AN IDENTIFIED ALLEGED FATHER, AND THE 30-DAY DEADLINE TO RESPOND
Once an alleged father is identified through the inquiry described in this document's companion clause, Family Code § 7666(a) requires that he actually be served with notice of the proceeding: "Except as provided in subdivision (b), notice of the proceeding shall be given to every person identified as the biological father or a possible biological father in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure for the service of process in a civil action in this state at least 10 days before the date of the proceeding, except that publication or posting of the notice of the proceeding is not required, and service on the parent or guardian of a biological father or possible biological father who is a minor is not required unless the minor has previously provided written authorization to serve the minor’s parent or guardian. Proof of giving the notice shall be filed with the court before the petition is heard." That notice starts a fixed statutory clock: under § 7666(b)(4), a man who "has been served with written notice of alleged parentage and the proposed adoption, and has failed to bring an action pursuant to subdivision (c) of Section 7630 within 30 days of service of the notice or the birth of the child, whichever is later," is, on that basis, no longer entitled to notice. A materially similar 30-day, notice-and-no-response condition appears, in almost the same words, as one of the statutory bases under § 7662(a)(2) on which a petition to terminate an alleged father's parental rights may proceed without his consent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b), notice of the proceeding shall be given to every person identified as the biological father or a possible biological father in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure for the service of process in a civil action in this state at least 10 days before the date of the proceeding, except that publication or posting of the notice of the proceeding is not required, and service on the parent or guardian of a biological father or possible biological father who is a minor is not required unless the minor has previously provided written authorization to serve the minor’s parent or guardian. Proof of giving the notice shall be filed with the court before the petition is heard."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7666(a) (California Legislative Information text), method and timing of notice to an identified alleged father (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7666.)
  "The alleged father has been served with written notice of alleged parentage and the proposed adoption, and has failed to bring an action pursuant to subdivision (c) of Section 7630 within 30 days of service of the notice or the birth of the child, whichever is later."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7666(b)(4) (California Legislative Information text), 30-day non-response basis for dispensing with further notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7666.)
  "The alleged father has been served as prescribed in Section 7666 with a written notice alleging that the alleged father is or could be the biological father of the child to be adopted or placed for adoption and has failed to bring an action for the purpose of declaring the existence of the father and child relationship pursuant to subdivision (c) of Section 7630 within 30 days of service of the notice or the birth of the child, whichever is later."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7662(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), the same 30-day non-response condition in the termination-petition context (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7662.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own notice mechanics and the specific 30-day response deadline that attaches once notice is actually served — not a claim about which state's law governs, or what notice or deadline, if any, another state's process applies to a specific child. This clause cites three provisions across two statutory sections: § 7666(a) and § 7666(b)(4) are subsections of the same section and are treated as one source; § 7662(a)(2) is a separate, independently numbered section restating a materially similar 30-day condition in a different procedural context (a petition to terminate parental rights, rather than an order dispensing with notice), and is treated as a second, independent source. This clause does not detail the separate general parentage action described in Family Code § 7630(c) itself — the action a timely response under this 30-day window would take the form of — which is addressed in this corpus's separate Paternity Action (Petition to Establish Parental Relationship) Information Sheet and its companion clauses, not restated here. This document is informational only: it does not itself serve notice on any specific alleged father, does not calculate whether any specific 30-day period has run, and does not determine that the alleged father named in this document's companion clauses has, or has not, brought a timely action.

THE ALLEGED FATHER'S OWN WRITTEN WAIVER OR DENIAL OF PARENTAGE
Separate from the consequence of failing to respond to notice within the statutory window, California law also gives an alleged father a direct, voluntary way to waive his own right to further notice. Family Code § 7662(a)(3) lists, among the circumstances under which a petition to terminate an alleged father's parental rights may proceed, that "The alleged father has executed a written form developed by the department to waive notice, to deny parentage, relinquish the child for adoption, or consent to the adoption of the child." Section 7662(b) describes the effect of that signed form directly: "The alleged father may validly execute a waiver or denial of parentage before or after the birth of the child, and, once signed, no notice of, relinquishment for, or consent to adoption of the child shall be required from the alleged father for the adoption to proceed." A materially similar waiver-or-denial mechanism also appears among the separate grounds on which a court may dispense with notice altogether under § 7666(b)(2).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The alleged father has executed a written form developed by the department to waive notice, to deny parentage, relinquish the child for adoption, or consent to the adoption of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7662(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), executed written waiver/denial as a basis to proceed without further notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7662.)
  "The alleged father may validly execute a waiver or denial of parentage before or after the birth of the child, and, once signed, no notice of, relinquishment for, or consent to adoption of the child shall be required from the alleged father for the adoption to proceed."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7662(b) (California Legislative Information text), effect of a validly executed waiver or denial of parentage (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7662.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California law provides a direct, voluntary mechanism by which an alleged father may himself waive notice or deny parentage — not a claim about which state's law governs, or whether any specific alleged father has executed, or would execute, such a waiver. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 7662(a)(3) and § 7662(b); they are treated as one source, not independent of each other. The cross-referenced, similarly worded mechanism in § 7666(b)(2) is noted for context but not independently re-quoted here, since it restates rather than adds to this same point. This document does not describe the department-developed form itself, its specific content, or where it may be obtained. This document is informational only: it does not itself waive, deny, relinquish, or consent to anything on behalf of the alleged father named in this document's companion clauses, and does not determine whether any specific waiver or denial is, or would be, validly executed.

WHEN NO ALLEGED FATHER CAN BE IDENTIFIED, AND THE STATUTORY HEARING DEADLINE
California's statutory scheme also addresses the situation in which the inquiry described in this document's companion clauses cannot identify any alleged father at all. Family Code § 7665 provides that, "If, after the inquiry, the court is unable to identify the biological father or any possible biological father and no person has appeared claiming to be the biological father and claiming custodial rights, the court shall enter an order terminating the unknown biological father’s parental rights with reference to the child." Where an alleged father has been identified, a separate timing rule applies to the petition itself: § 7667(a) provides that "Notwithstanding any other law, an action to terminate the parental rights of an alleged father of a child as specified in this part shall be set for hearing not more than 45 days after filing of the petition, except as provided in subdivision (c)." That exception, in § 7667(c), lets the court dispense with a hearing altogether in specific circumstances, including under § 7667(c)(1) where "The identity or whereabouts of the alleged father are unknown."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If, after the inquiry, the court is unable to identify the biological father or any possible biological father and no person has appeared claiming to be the biological father and claiming custodial rights, the court shall enter an order terminating the unknown biological father’s parental rights with reference to the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7665 (California Legislative Information text), termination of an unknown biological father's parental rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7665.)
  "Notwithstanding any other law, an action to terminate the parental rights of an alleged father of a child as specified in this part shall be set for hearing not more than 45 days after filing of the petition, except as provided in subdivision (c)."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7667(a) (California Legislative Information text), 45-day hearing deadline for a termination petition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7667.)
  "The identity or whereabouts of the alleged father are unknown."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7667(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), ex parte termination where identity or whereabouts are unknown (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7667.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's own text handles an alleged father who cannot be identified at all, and of the deadline and ex parte exception that apply to the termination petition itself — not a claim about which state's law governs, or what happens, if any, under another state's process when a specific alleged father cannot be identified or located. This clause cites three statutory provisions: § 7665 is a single, independently numbered section, cited as one source; § 7667(a) and § 7667(c)(1) are subsections of a second, separate section and are treated together as a second source. This clause does not restate § 7667(c)(2)-(3)'s other two ex parte grounds — a validly executed waiver, addressed in this document's companion clause on the alleged father's own waiver, and the 30-day non-response condition, addressed in this document's companion clause on notice and the response deadline — to avoid re-quoting citations already independently verified elsewhere in this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any alleged father named, or not named, in this document's companion clauses is unidentifiable, and does not schedule, waive, or dispense with any hearing.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — NOTICE TO ALLEGED FATHER INFORMATION SHEET
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on September 5, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for background use alongside an actual adoption proceeding, or a petition to terminate the parental rights of an alleged father under Family Code § 7662, filed with the California superior court. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete any such filing, does not conduct the inquiry described in this document's companion clauses, does not give or receive notice on behalf of any party, and does not waive, terminate, or preserve any person's parental rights; only the statutory process described in those clauses, and a final court order, can do that.]

citations.quote: The alleged father may validly execute a waiver or denial of parentage before or after the birth of the child, and, once signed, no notice of, relinquishment for, or consent to adoption of the child shall be required from the alleged father for the adoption to proceed.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California law provides a direct, voluntary mechanism by which an alleged father may himself waive notice or deny parentage — not a claim about which state's law governs, or whether any specific alleged father has executed, or would execute, such a waiver. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 7662(a)(3) and § 7662(b); they are treated as one source, not independent of each other. The cross-referenced, similarly worded mechanism in § 7666(b)(2) is noted for context but not independently re-quoted here, since it restates rather than adds to this same point. This document does not describe the department-developed form itself, its specific content, or where it may be obtained. This document is informational only: it does not itself waive, deny, relinquish, or consent to anything on behalf of the alleged father named in this document's companion clauses, and does not determine whether any specific waiver or denial is, or would be, validly executed.

expectedJSON.body: California's statutory scheme also addresses the situation in which the inquiry described in this document's companion clauses cannot identify any alleged father at all. Family Code § 7665 provides that, "If, after the inquiry, the court is unable to identify the biological father or any possible biological father and no person has appeared claiming to be the biological father and claiming custodial rights, the court shall enter an order terminating the unknown biological father’s parental rights with reference to the child." Where an alleged father has been identified, a separate timing rule applies to the petition itself: § 7667(a) provides that "Notwithstanding any other law, an action to terminate the parental rights of an alleged father of a child as specified in this part shall be set for hearing not more than 45 days after filing of the petition, except as provided in subdivision (c)." That exception, in § 7667(c), lets the court dispense with a hearing altogether in specific circumstances, including under § 7667(c)(1) where "The identity or whereabouts of the alleged father are unknown."

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's own text handles an alleged father who cannot be identified at all, and of the deadline and ex parte exception that apply to the termination petition itself — not a claim about which state's law governs, or what happens, if any, under another state's process when a specific alleged father cannot be identified or located. This clause cites three statutory provisions: § 7665 is a single, independently numbered section, cited as one source; § 7667(a) and § 7667(c)(1) are subsections of a second, separate section and are treated together as a second source. This clause does not restate § 7667(c)(2)-(3)'s other two ex parte grounds — a validly executed waiver, addressed in this document's companion clause on the alleged father's own waiver, and the 30-day non-response condition, addressed in this document's companion clause on notice and the response deadline — to avoid re-quoting citations already independently verified elsewhere in this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any alleged father named, or not named, in this document's companion clauses is unidentifiable, and does not schedule, waive, or dispense with any hearing.
